latest.title: UK cost of living squeeze tightens as mortgage rates rise ; JLR announces 4,000 job cuts – business live
latest.summary: Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news UK house prices fall for first time in nearly three years, says Lloyds The rise in mortgage rates could cool demand in the UK housing market, where ( as reported earlier) prices fell last month. Tom Bill, head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, says: “We have seen a spring slump rather than a seasonal bounce this year as prices and transactions came under pressure from higher mortgage costs and an ever-present concern around which taxes the government may raise next. Falling house prices are a natural consequence of that and whether we see a seasonal autumn bounce will depend on the level of any pre-Budget speculation and how the unpredictable conflict in the Middle East unfolds and impacts on UK inflation expectations.” The average 2-year fixed residential mortgage rate today is 5.63%. This is up from 5.60% the previous working day. The average 5-year fixed residential mortgage rate today is 5.68%. This is up from 5.64% the previous working day. “The pricing margins among major lenders are under pressure due to renewed volatility in the swap rate market, so it is somewhat inevitable for them to adjust rates. Major lenders, which include HSBC and NatWest, have increased rates since the start of September. The recent uplift in swap rates has started to filter into the pricing of fixed rate mortgages, with more moves expected in the coming days. Swap rates are much higher than they were a month ago and are a key influence on how lenders price their fixed-rate mortgages. Lenders look at margins very carefully, so it would be unwise to price their deals too low, if the expectations are for interest rates to rise, even if over the short-term. “Mortgage rates are rising due to the escalating military conflict between the US and Iran, reigniting inflationary fears. The UK 10-year gilt yield has also risen further above 5% to an 18-year high recently due to a global bond sell-off, adding further pressure to the wholesale funding costs that underpin fixed mortgage pricing. However, the hit to the mortgage market over recent days pales in comparison to when the conflict in the Middle East began around six months ago, when many lenders pulled fixed rate deals. While this alone might still not reassure some borrowers, it is worth noting that the pressure on swap rates over the past six months has not been caused by UK fiscal policy, which is why withdrawals and rate hikes are nowhere near the scale experienced in the aftermath of the ‘mini-Budget’ in 2022. Continue reading...

latest.title: Being ‘true to Labour’s values’ means controlling spending, says Healey – UK politics live
latest.summary: Chancellor says there’s ‘nothing progressive’ about government spending £1 in every ten on debt interest Chancellor to argue UK economy can ‘turn corner’ despite bond market turmoil Healey says Andy Burnham set out in his statement to MPs last week what he thought had gone wrong The fundamentals of our economy [were] hollowed out through a series of past policy decisions, political power was centralised, weakening the relationships between the people, the businesses and the institutions who can make things happen beyond Whitehall. The economic enablers were privatised and outsourced, leaving accountability to a thicket of arm’s length bodies and regulators, too often without the predictability or the pace that underpins a thriving market economy. And our country was deindustrialised as the cost to make anything, to build anything here soared, and our dependence on unreliable sources grew, including in areas critical to our national security and sovereignty. Let me be clear, I recognise that the costs of business, its energy bills, regulation, burdens, planning constraints, labour costs, have grown since Covid and I want to draw the line. And whether it is the cost of business or the cost of living, the only way we deal with these in the long term is growth. Continue reading...

Sports.summary: From home-run celebrations to tilted caps, players embracing joy continue to collide with an old guard devoted to Dust Bowl grimness Over the last several years, simultaneously lauded and paralyzed by its ironclad traditions, baseball has undergone various forays into reinvention, trying to free itself from its unwritten rules of retaliation , its seeming aversion to joy, its demand that every generation of player of every culture and background play the game with the grimness of a Dust Bowl farmer. The sport even attempted to change those customs by promoting a cultural shift with an industry-wide motto : Let the Kids Play. But in a time of intense division within the aggressive backdrop of Trumpism, the result is a racial clash that is actually a generational and cultural one that predates current politics by a century. Sports.title: Will hordes of influencers, weed smokers and mid-point talkers bring down the US Open?
Sports.summary: This year, the noise at the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center has officially become A Problem. But changing it would mean changing society The first thing you notice while sitting in the upper tiers of Arthur Ashe Stadium is the noise. A persistent exterior hum filters up from ground level, fed by the massive ventilation and cooling units that sit outside the stadium, the clack of the Long Island Rail Road to the north, and the forklifts receiving goods from the refrigerator trucks that keep the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center flush with its essential supplies of Evian, champagne, and premium IPA. Overhead, planes descending toward LaGuardia airport ensure the auditory assault takes place by land and air simultaneously. In the lower rakes of the stadium, the babble of the spectators is incessant; it’s not unusual to overhear full-volume conversations on various non-tennis topics – work, family, romance, last night’s dinner – that continue without interruption for the duration of an entire match. New York is famously noisy, and the US Open, as the most glamorous annual sporting event in town, has always been loud in sympathy with its environment. Indeed, the brashness of the American grand slam has historically been its major selling point, the signature that distinguishes it from the Australian Open (the “happy slam”), Wimbledon (strawberries and cream, all-white attire, the home of tennis), and the French Open (French). People have been complaining about the volume of the New York crowd for decades. But this year the noise at the US Open feels different. This year noise at the noisy slam has become A Problem. Culture.title: Primetime review – Robert Pattinson’s preening TV host hunts paedophiles but real drama proves harder to target
Culture.summary: Venice film festival: Lance Oppenheim’s drama about controversial US reality show To Catch a Predator is unsure what it wants to say about media or morality Lance Oppenheim is the acclaimed documentary-maker who has made his feature debut with a strangely overwrought and heavy-footed drama-thriller, which for all its elaborate neon-lit atmosphere of noir danger isn’t at all sure what it wants to say about media or morality, or anything else. The subject is the controversial top-rated US TV reality show To Catch a Predator which ran from 2004 to 2008; that title was evidently taken from the Hitchcock movie To Catch a Thief, which in turn was inspired by the phrase “Set a thief to catch a thief”. In search of prey, the show’s researchers baited paedophiles in online chatrooms posing as children, lured them to “sting houses” where actors played underage teens on the front porch to get the abusers inside, where they can be clearly filmed expressing criminal intentions. But before anything could happen, sonorous host Chris Hansen appeared from nowhere and confronted these cringing abusers – which made for fantastic television. After this the cops made an arrest, and they and the state prosecutor did the heavy lifting of overseeing due process and presumably debating the merits of entrapment in court, although this obvious issue is not raised in the movie. Culture.title: Imperium review – Sergei Loznitsa’s archive collage collates everyday life in cold-war Soviet Union
Culture.summary: Venice film festival: The Two Prosecutors director cuts together documentary footage shot by a TV crew in the 1970s to try and get across what daily life in the USSR was like Here is an archive-compilation documentary from Sergei Loznitsa, a hypnotic panorama of early 1970s life across the vast reaches of the Soviet Union, or maybe we should call it the Soviet empire. Loznitsa gives it the Latin title Imperium, perhaps to recall the Romans before their decline and fall. His material is taken from fascinating footage shot between 1970 and 1973 by a visiting Italian camera crew who presumably had the necessary permissions and were well enough liked by the authorities to keep coming back. The effect is part Potemkin village, part seance, part ethnographic study; there are no interviews or voiceover, just ambient footage. (The Italians may have intended this material as B-roll to be fitted into a more conventional film.) Imperium has sometimes the eerie quality of a ghost story with phantoms drifting placidly across the screen, gazing blankly into the camera, occasionally grimacing or grinning, but destined never to see the film of which they are a part. We don’t see the gulags, of course, or really anything like agencies of the state, apart from the soldiers at the October Revolution parades in Red Square. Many of the former Soviet state capitals featured here nowadays have tourist-attraction KGB museums based in their brutal former HQs; that kind of thing is obviously absent here. Continue reading...
